clinicalPearls: Entrapment or compression of the superficial (sensory) branch of the radial nerve over the distal radial forearm and wrist, producing purely sensory symptoms over the dorsoradial hand.
Patients describe pain, numbness and tingling over the dorsum of the thumb and dorsoradial hand, often provoked by tight wristbands, watch straps or handcuffs.
Because the branch is purely sensory, there is no motor weakness and no wrist drop, distinguishing it from a radial nerve or posterior interosseous lesion.
The nerve becomes subcutaneous as it emerges between brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus, where forearm pronation can pinch it (a scissoring mechanism).
A Tinel sign over the distal radial forearm and a positive response to forced pronation and ulnar wrist flexion support the diagnosis.
Overlap with de Quervain tenosynovitis is common, and the two may coexist, so the first dorsal compartment should be examined carefully.
Symptoms frequently follow external compression, direct trauma, or surgery and cannula placement in the region.
Sensory nerve conduction studies of the superficial radial nerve, compared with the asymptomatic side, help confirm the lesion.
reference.pathophysiology: The superficial radial nerve travels beneath brachioradialis in the forearm and emerges to become subcutaneous roughly at the junction of the middle and distal thirds, passing over the tendons of the first dorsal compartment to supply sensation to the dorsoradial hand and dorsum of the thumb and adjacent fingers. Forearm pronation causes the tendons of brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus to scissor across the nerve, and external circumferential pressure, direct trauma or local scarring produce focal demyelination and axonal irritation. As the branch carries no motor fibres, the clinical picture is confined to sensory disturbance and pain.
additionalDifferentials: posterior interosseous or radial tunnel syndrome
additionalInvestigations: superficial radial sensory nerve conduction studies with contralateral comparison
high-resolution ultrasound of the superficial radial nerve in the distal forearm
magnetic resonance imaging if a mass or structural lesion is suspected
wrist and thumb radiographs to assess the carpometacarpal joint
diagnostic local anaesthetic block of the superficial radial nerve
cervical spine imaging when radiculopathy is a consideration
examination for coexisting de Quervain tenosynovitis with the Finkelstein manoeuvre
redFlags: any true motor weakness, which indicates a more proximal radial nerve lesion rather than this sensory syndrome
a progressive or palpable mass along the nerve course suggesting a peripheral nerve tumour
features of complex regional pain syndrome such as trophic and vasomotor change
multifocal sensory symptoms suggesting a generalised or inflammatory neuropathy
reference.prognosis: Removal of external compression and conservative treatment resolve symptoms in most cases, and the outlook is generally good. Refractory or post-traumatic cases may need neurolysis, though painful neuroma and persistent dysaesthesia can complicate recovery.
pitfalls: mistaking the sensory symptoms for de Quervain tenosynovitis and overlooking coexistence of the two
attributing motor findings to this syndrome, which is by definition purely sensory
failing to identify a modifiable external compressive source such as a tight strap or handcuffs
generating a painful neuroma through surgical intervention in a poorly selected case
references: Dawson, Hallett and Wilbourn: Entrapment Neuropathies
